_comment: The pinned baseline. Every experiment is one deliberate change from this,
with everything else identical, so a difference in the results table can be
attributed to the thing that was changed. Do not edit these values to chase
a better number - make a new config, give it a run_id, and record both rows.
Chosen before server access landed, so it is deliberately the configuration
most likely to run anywhere: 1.7B fully fine-tuned fits a single 24GB card
in bf16 with gradient checkpointing and an 8-bit optimiser.

model.name: Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B
why: Small enough to FULLY fine-tune, which is the point of this phase - LoRA
on 7B updates too few parameters for ~700 training conversations' worth
of turns to move the model far from its pretraining.
Apache 2.0, so no license friction for a university project.
Strong instruction following at its size, which matters because the model
must emit a Strategy line and a Response in a fixed shape.
Qwen3 ships one instruct-tuned repo per size with no -Instruct suffix;
'Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B-Instruct' does not exist on the Hub. Use Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B.
model.dtype: float16 with fp32 master - no native bf16 on this cluster

format_note: case1 (text only) immediately followed by case2 (text + physiological
summary) for the same turn. Chosen as the baseline because it is the
arrangement that most obviously teaches the model that the physiological
summary is optional context for the same input, rather than a different
kind of example. Batched and randomised are the experiment.
loss_note: Mask the prompt; compute loss only from '### Response:' to <EOS>.
Two reasons, the second is the one that matters for our experiment:
1. The completion is 43% of a case1 string but only 22% of a case2 string,
and a fixed 417-character instruction header repeats on all 993 turns.
Unmasked, most of the gradient goes into reproducing boilerplate.
2. Because that prompt/completion ratio differs between case1 and case2,
unmasked loss weights the two cases differently by construction - which
would confound the data-formatting comparison before it starts.

notes: 1e-5 rather than the 2e-4 usual for LoRA - full fine-tuning moves every
weight, so the LoRA learning rate would wreck the model at this data size.
3 epochs on 1420 training strings is roughly 265 optimiser steps at an
effective batch of 16. Watch validation loss: with data this small,
overfitting after epoch 2 is the expected failure, not the exception.
checkpoint_selection: eval_loss on the validation split, at each epoch. The run keeps the best
epoch in final/, not the last one - validation loss bottoms at epoch 1 on
this corpus and rises afterwards, so the last checkpoint is the worst of
the three. epochs stays at 3 so that every run reports where its own
minimum was, rather than assuming the baseline's answer holds for a

generation.note: Greedy for scoring. Two runs of the same checkpoint must give the same score, or the table is measuring sampling noise.

evaluation.harness_status: not started - no code in the repo as of 3 Sep 2026
evaluation.credit_rule: harness_assigned_to records who the split gave it to, not who wrote it. Whoever writes it gets named in RESULTS.md as its author. Same rule as the run rows: the owner column is who did the work, not who was pencilled in for it.

why: gpupart_v100 (gnode1) is the only partition that can fully fine-tune
anything in our size range. gpupart_p100 (gnode2-5) is 16GB and
gpupart_q4000 (gnode6-8) is 8GB Quadro P4000 - note that the 48-hour
partition is the 8GB one, so the longest queue is attached to the cards
that cannot hold a 1B model under full fine-tuning.
No card on the cluster is Ampere: compute capability tops out at 7.0, so
there is no native bf16 anywhere and every run pays the fp32 master copy,
about 12 bytes/param rather than 6. train.py detects this by compute
capability, not by torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported(), which returns True on
a V100 because it counts emulated bf16.
8-bit optimiser states are load-bearing: 26GB against 38GB for the
baseline, on a 32GB card.
